Basal metabolic rate measurements in the Southern tuco-tuco (Ctenomys australis) were obtained from respirometry trials conducted under standard thermoneutral conditions. During these experiments, which were carried out at a body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], the maximum oxygen consumption recorded reached 146.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 146.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This value reflects the energetic demands of a relatively large subterranean rodent that must cope with the high costs of digging through compacted soils. Compared to other ctenomyids of similar body mass, this basal metabolic rate is consistent with the typical endothermic requirements of fossorial mammals, though slightly elevated relative to some surface-dwelling rodents of comparable size. The measurements were taken from adult individuals that had been acclimated to laboratory conditions and were resting quietly within a darkened metabolic chamber, ensuring that the recorded values approximated true basal metabolism rather than resting or routine metabolic rates.

Neonatal body mass in this species has been inferred from closely related congeners, given the practical difficulties of obtaining precise birth weights from wild burrow systems. Based on allometric relationships derived from Ctenomys talarum, the estimated wet weight at birth is 22.9 grams [Wwb = 22.9 grams]. This relatively modest neonatal mass is typical of altricial rodent young, which are born in a comparatively undeveloped state and require an extended period of maternal investment before they become independent. The pattern of small birth masses coupled with extended parental care appears to be a widespread strategy among subterranean rodents, where the energetic costs of burrow construction and thermoregulation place strong selective pressures on reproductive allocation. Field observations of neonatal litters in Ctenomys australis remain scarce, but the inferred value provides a useful baseline for comparative analyses of life-history strategies within the genus.

Adult body size in Southern tuco-tucos reaches an asymptotic mass of approximately 347 grams [Wwi = approximately 347 grams], based on measurements from a sample of reproductively mature individuals captured in coastal dune habitats of Buenos Aires Province. Reported field values typically range between 349 and 366 grams, indicating that the ultimate wet weight may vary modestly depending on local resource availability and population density. Females generally attain slightly smaller maximum masses than males, a pattern consistent with the mild sexual dimorphism observed across many Ctenomys species. This absolute mass places Ctenomys australis among the medium-sized members of its genus, distinctly larger than the smaller Ctenomys talarum yet considerably smaller than the giant tuco-tuco species found further north. The attainment of adult body mass is a gradual process that extends well beyond the weaning period.

During this suckling juvenile stage, the young grow rapidly within the sheltered confines of the maternal burrow system, protected from surface predators and environmental extremes. The extended gestation and lactation periods together represent a considerable reproductive investment that is offset by the relatively large litters and the low metabolic costs of remaining underground. Field data from related species suggest that reproductive output is timed to coincide with seasonal peaks in resource availability.

The life-history trajectory of Ctenomys australis is characterized by a comparatively slow pace for a rodent, with sexual maturation occurring at approximately 243 days after birth [tp = approximately 243 days after birth] under the thermoneutral conditions typical of active metabolic periods at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. Females reach puberty considerably later than many surface-dwelling murids, reflecting the energetic constraints imposed by a fossorial lifestyle. Once reproductive maturity is attained, females typically produce litters ranging from 2 to 6 pups [N_R_i = litters ranging from 2 to 6 pups], with an average annual reproductive frequency of approximately 1.5 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 1.5 litters per year]. The maximum recorded lifespan in the wild has been estimated at 730 days [am = 730 days] at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], though captive individuals may persist somewhat longer under favorable conditions. This combination of delayed maturation, moderate litter sizes, and relatively short lifespan places Ctenomys australis firmly within the slow end of the fast-slow continuum for mammals of its body size, a life-history strategy that is further reinforced by the high energetic costs of burrow excavation and thermoregulation in the subterranean niche.
